paths.title: Make a website
paths.tagline: A page for your org, a portfolio, an event site.
paths.language_reason: Every web page starts as HTML, so you'll see your page in a browser from day one. CSS and JavaScript come next to style it and make it react.

paths.title: Automate boring tasks
paths.tagline: Rename files, tidy spreadsheets, make small helper tools.
paths.language_reason: Python reads almost like English and can rename files, read spreadsheets and fill in forms with a few lines, so you can automate a real chore early.

paths.title: Work with data
paths.tagline: Sort, count and answer questions about real data, like survey results.
paths.language_reason: Python is the most common beginner language for working with data, and SQL is how you ask a database questions. Python comes first because it teaches the basics both use.

paths.title: Learn databases
paths.tagline: Store and look up records, like an org's members or a sari-sari store's stock.
paths.language_reason: SQL is the language almost every database understands. It's short and readable, and you don't need another language first.

paths.title: Make games and fun projects
paths.language_reason: Python lets you make a working text game in your first week without installing a game engine. JavaScript comes after, to put games in a browser.

paths.title: Get ahead in CS class
paths.tagline: Feel ready for programming classes and exams.
paths.language_reason: Most first-year programming classes start with Python or Java. Python builds the habits; Java then shows the stricter style many classes grade on.

paths.title: Start from zero
paths.tagline: The ideas every language shares, before you pick one.
paths.language_reason: These ideas work in any language. The examples use Python because it reads almost like English.
